questions.q: In sys.dm_tran_locks, what does a request_status of WAIT mean?
options: The session is queued behind another session's incompatible lock on that resource
The lock request has permanently failed
The session currently holds the lock
The resource no longer exists
questions.explain: GRANT means the session holds the lock; WAIT means it's queued behind an incompatible lock held by someone else.

questions.q: Which lock mode is compatible with nothing else, including another instance of itself?
options: X (Exclusive)
S (Shared)
IS (Intent Shared)
U (Update)
questions.explain: Exclusive locks are fully incompatible with all other lock modes — that incompatibility is the root of most blocking.

questions.q: What is the purpose of intent locks like IS and IX?
options: They're placed at a higher level (like a table) to signal a lock exists lower down, so SQL Server doesn't have to scan every row to check for conflicts
They replace shared and exclusive locks entirely
They only apply to system databases
They prevent any locking from occurring at all
questions.explain: Intent locks are an efficiency mechanism — they let SQL Server check for conflicts at the table level before drilling into rows.

questions.q: Which column in sys.dm_exec_requests identifies the session responsible for blocking the current request?
options: blocking_session_id
wait_type
resource_associated_entity_id
transaction_id
questions.explain: blocking_session_id names the session ID that's blocking the current request, or 0 if it isn't blocked.

questions.q: In a five-session blocking chain, which session should you investigate first?
options: The head of the chain — the session blocking others but not itself blocked
The last session in the chain, since it waited longest
Whichever session has the lowest session_id number
It doesn't matter — killing any session clears the whole chain
questions.explain: Everyone behind the head of the chain is just waiting on it; fixing or killing the head resolves the rest.
